Thought: I need to determine what happens when oximes are hydrolyzed. Oximes have the general structure R₁R₂C=NOH, where R₁ and R₂ are organic groups (and one of them can be hydrogen in the case of aldoximes).

When oximes undergo hydrolysis (typically in acidic conditions), they break down into their original carbonyl compounds (ketones or aldehydes) and release hydroxylamine (NH₂OH), which can further decompose to ammonia (NH₃) under certain conditions.

The reaction is essentially the reverse of oxime formation:
R₁R₂C=NOH + H₂O → R₁R₂C=O + NH₂OH

Under acidic conditions, the hydroxylamine can further decompose to ammonia:
NH₂OH → NH₃ + [O]

Looking at the options:
A. Carboxylic acids and amines - This is incorrect; oximes don't typically hydrolyze to carboxylic acids
B. Esters and water - This is incorrect; esters are not formed in oxime hydrolysis
C. Ketones/aldehydes and ammonia - This is correct if we consider the complete decomposition where hydroxylamine further breaks down to ammonia
D. Ketones/aldehydes and hydroxylamines - This is the direct product of oxime hydrolysis

The most accurate answer is C, as the main decomposition products of oxime hydrolysis are ketones/aldehydes and ammonia (after the hydroxylamine decomposes).
Final Answer: [ANSWER]C[/ANSWER]
